summary:
Recombination frequency is the share of offspring with a reshuffled combination of two loci. It returns recombination frequency, map distance, parental offspring and recombinant : parental, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It is both the map distance in centimorgans and the experimental quantity a three-point cross measures, so this calculator converts between counts, percentage, map units and the testcross classes that produced them. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Recombination Frequency
sections.html:
RF (%) = recombinant offspring ÷ total offspring × 100

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
recombinantoffspring with a new allele combinationindividuals
totalall offspring scoredindividuals
RFrecombination frequency, equal to map units in cM%

sections.title: How do I use the Recombination Frequency?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: recombinant offspring of 84 individuals, total offspring of 400 individuals.

Substituting them into the formula gives recombination frequency of 21%, map distance of 21 cM, parental offspring of 316 individuals, recombinant : parental of 0.2658 :1.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
below 50%Linkedthe loci are on the same chromosome
about 50%Independentunlinked, or so far apart they assort freely
near 0%Tightly linkedvery few crossovers between the loci

  • Only a testcross (one parent homozygous recessive) exposes the recombinant classes directly; in an F2 cross the recombinants are masked by dominance.

  • Small samples give noisy estimates: with 100 offspring, one recombinant is a whole percentage point.

  • A single recombination frequency cannot be greater than 50%, which is why long intervals are measured as sums of short ones.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Scoring an F2 instead of a testcross and expecting the recombinants to be visible.
  • Adding frequencies from overlapping intervals.
  • Forgetting that in a three-point cross each double crossover is counted twice.

faq.q: What is the difference between recombination frequency and map distance?
faq.a: They are numerically equal below about 10 cM; beyond that map distance uses a mapping function to correct for unseen double crossovers.
The loci assort independently — either they are on different chromosomes or far enough apart on the same one.

faq.q: What does the Recombination Frequency actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns recombination frequency, map distance, parental offspring and recombinant : parental. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
